Thorough experimental analysis including behavior shift analysis, nuanced cost-effectiveness evaluation, and per-repository breakdown revealing the relationship between commit history availability and performance gains

Arbitrary hyperparameter choices (7,000 commits, top-200 files) without ablation studies or sensitivity analysis to justify selections

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly articulates a genuine limitation in existing approaches (treating every problem from scratch) with effective illustrative examples
Practical solution: Simple, straightforward memory mechanisms (BM25 search + LLM summaries) that are easy to implement and integrate into existing frameworks
Solid empirical improvements: Consistent gains across benchmarks (~4.9% absolute improvement on SWE-bench-verified); ablations show both components contribute meaningfully

Insightful analysis: Good per-repository breakdown showing correlation with commit history, tool use distribution analysis revealing behavioral shifts, and cost-effectiveness analysis demonstrating strategic resource allocation
Retrieval insights: Interesting finding that sparse methods significantly outperform dense retrieval on code, with broader implications for code understanding tasks
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with good motivation, clear figures, concrete examples, and logical flow
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core contribution applies two standard techniques (BM25 + LLM summaries) in a straightforward manner. Neither memory mechanism is novel—primarily an engineering contribution rather than advancing the state-of-the-art
Unjustified hyperparameter choices: Why 200 files for semantic memory? Why 7,000 commits? No ablations, sensitivity analysis, or principled justifications provided

Significant failure mode on small repositories: Table 2 shows -13.1% performance drop on repos with sparse history, undermining general applicability. No solutions proposed despite acknowledging this critical limitation

Incomplete methodology documentation: File summary generation procedure unspecified (LLM? Prompt?), 'LLM-based tokenizer' for BM25 never explained, contamination filtering threshold unclear. These gaps severely impede reproducibility

Limited evaluation scope: Only file-level localization (not actual bug fixing); SWE-bench-live uses only 130 filtered examples (down from 500); no evaluation on related tasks; no error bars or significance testing reported

Unpredictable cost increases: Figure 4 shows high variance in per-example costs. While framed as strategic investment, the unpredictability is concerning for practitioners. Average costs increase despite improved accuracy
Sparse retrieval quality analysis: Dense vs. sparse comparison only on django; explanation for sparse dominance is speculative; no per-repository error analysis; BM25 tokenization details absent
Insufficient error analysis: Described as 'small-scale' without specifying sample sizes; failure modes identified but not quantified; no principled method to predict when memory helps vs. hurts
Missing baselines: No comparison with simpler approaches (e.g., commits without summaries) or other memory-augmented methods mentioned in related work
Reproducibility issues: No code release mentioned, implementation details scattered/missing, summary generation unspecified, memory size/efficiency not discussed
No statistical significance testing: Single-run results without error bars or confidence intervals; concerning given cost variance shown in Figure 4
Hyperparameter sensitivity unclear: Retrieval method comparison limited to one repository; generalizability of findings questionable

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies and illustrates (Figure 2) how repository memory addresses a genuine limitation of memoryless agents
Elegant solution design: simple, practical mechanisms (BM25 commit search, commit-frequency semantic memory) that integrate cleanly into LocAgent without architectural changes
Strong empirical results: consistent 4.9% absolute improvement on SWE-bench-verified, with gains on SWE-bench-live; proper ablations show both memory types contribute

Thorough analysis beyond metrics: behavioral shift analysis (Figure 3) demonstrates strategic change to hypothesis-driven investigation; detailed cost analysis (Figure 4) shows problem-dependent efficiency; retrieval method comparison validates sparse>dense for code
Clear contribution with practical value: addresses real limitation, simple to implement and integrate, honest error analysis identifying failure modes
Strong reproducibility: detailed implementation specs, comprehensive tool documentation, explicit leakage prevention measures
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components (BM25 retrieval, commit frequency, LLM summarization) are straightforward applications of existing techniques; integration is additive rather than architecturally novel
Insufficient hyperparameter justification: key choices (7K commits, 200 files) lack ablation studies or sensitivity analysis; generalization to different-scale repositories unclear

Shallow analysis of failure modes: error analysis acknowledged as 'small-scale'; degraded performance on low-history repos explained speculatively without systematic characterization of when/why memory helps

Narrow evaluation scope: only SWE-bench variants (mature projects with good commit history); unclear performance on younger projects, forks, or poor-quality commits; SWE-bench-live uses only 130 examples
Incomplete cost analysis: ~60% cost increase on failed examples not fully contextualized; pre-computing semantic memory cost not discussed; aggregate benchmark cost unclear
Retrieval method validation limited to single repository: sparse vs. dense analysis (Table 4) based only on django; generalization to other repos unverified
Unaddressed scalability and staleness concerns: memory degradation over time, very large repository handling, and emergence of important new modules not in top-200 historical files
Missing comparisons: no baseline with simpler alternatives (e.g., just augmenting with top-changed files); limited discussion of relationships to other SE approaches using commit history
Scope limited to localization: no evaluation on full bug-fixing pipeline; unclear how localization improvements translate to actual bug fixes

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clear articulation of memory limitation in agents, effectively illustrated through Django migration failure case (Figure 2)
Solid experimental results: Consistent improvements on both SWE-bench-verified (76.5% vs 71.6%, +4.9%) and SWE-bench-live (66.2% vs 63.1%), with positive ablations showing both components contribute

Thoughtful empirical analysis: Comprehensive investigation including behavior shift analysis (Figure 3), cost-effectiveness breakdown (Table 3), retrieval method comparison (Table 4), per-repository performance breakdown (Table 2), and honest error analysis

Practical design with good integration: Modular memory mechanisms integrate cleanly with LocAgent without major framework modifications; two complementary memory types (episodic + semantic) sensibly designed
Strong reproducibility: Detailed implementation documentation (§4.1), comprehensive appendices with tool examples and prompts, and promise of code release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Memory mechanisms are straightforward (BM25 retrieval, frequency-based file selection), closely mirroring JiT-SDP literature; adding tools to agentic frameworks is incremental rather than novel

Fundamental dependency on repository history: Performance degrades significantly on sparse-history repos (Table 2: 54.3% vs 67.4%), with no principled mechanism to detect novelty or fall back; approach inapplicable to novel bugs unrelated to past commits

Semantic memory construction concerns: Frequency-based file selection is simplistic; circular evaluation (LocAgent generates summaries, then LocAgent+memory evaluated); only 83.1% coverage of target files in top-200 active (Table 5); no analysis of summary quality or hallucinations

Limited evaluation scope: Only tested on LocAgent (unclear generalization to Agentless or other frameworks); SWE-bench-live subset small (130 examples); all Python projects; file-level only; sensitivity analysis limited to Django repo

Retrieval quality inadequately validated: Relies on imperfect explicit commit-issue links; BM25 can retrieve distracting irrelevant commits (acknowledged via Figure 4 high variance); error analysis small-scale (§4.3); no systematic study of when memory hurts

Experimental design limitations: Fixed hyperparameters (K=200, 7000 commits) applied uniformly despite known variability; no comparison of alternative memory strategies (time-decay, developer experience, co-change patterns); no statistical significance testing; no analysis of scaling with repo size/age

Non-negligible cost overhead: Average cost increases 11-50% (Table 3), especially for failing cases; while justified on difficult problems, overall cost-benefit tradeoff and guidance for practical use underexplored

Generalization concerns: Evaluation limited to mature, open-source Python projects with rich histories; applicability to private codebases, other languages, young/new repositories, or cross-repository scenarios unclear or likely limited

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear illustration of limitations in current approaches
Comprehensive empirical evaluation with proper ablations on two benchmarks and detailed analysis
Consistent improvements across benchmarks (4.9% on verified, 3.1% on live) with evidence of shifted agent behavior
Practical modular design that integrates cleanly with existing frameworks
Thorough analysis including cost-effectiveness, per-repository breakdown, and downstream task impact
Good reproducibility with detailed implementation details and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited novelty: straightforward application of existing techniques (BM25 retrieval, LLM summaries) to existing method (LocAgent); core ideas not new

Significant failure modes inadequately addressed: 13.1% degradation on sparse-history repositories with no concrete mitigation strategy or detection mechanism
Heuristic memory construction: top-200 file selection is simplistic with only 83.1% coverage; no sophisticated temporal filtering despite citing JiT-SDP literature
Modest improvements relative to baselines: only 5.1% absolute gain over Agentless (71.4%) on verified benchmark; performance even weaker on live benchmark

Limited evaluation scope: 12 total repositories, heavily filtered SWE-bench-live subset (130 examples), no comparison with other recent agentic frameworks
Missing critical ablations: time-decay effects, bug-type analysis, commit message quality impact, and detailed understanding of when memory helps vs. hurts

Insufficient engagement with related work: no empirical comparison with other memory-augmented approaches; acknowledged connection to JiT-SDP not deeply explored

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: Identifies genuine limitation in current agents (lack of long-term repository memory) with effective examples (Figure 2)
Practical and modular solution: Simple memory mechanisms integrate cleanly into existing frameworks without major modifications
Comprehensive evaluation: Multiple benchmarks, strong baselines, thorough ablations, per-repository analysis, downstream impact assessment, and efficiency analysis
Consistent empirical improvements: +4.9% on SWE-bench-verified and +3.1% on SWE-bench-live across all baselines
Insightful analysis: Behavioral shifts (Figure 3), strategic cost allocation (Tables 3-4), surprising superiority of sparse retrieval, and honest failure mode discussion
Good reproducibility: Detailed implementation details, comprehensive appendices with prompts and documentation, commitment to code release
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core contribution is incremental—primarily applies known JiT-SDP techniques (commit history, code churn signals) to memory-augmented agents without algorithmic innovation
Critical repository-dependency limitation: Performance degrades significantly on sparse-history repositories (Table 2: -13.1% on 'others' group), severely limiting generalizability

Memory construction concerns: Relies on noisy/missing explicit commit-issue links; fixed 7,000-commit window is simplistic; semantic memory generation costs scalability unclear; no update/maintenance strategy
Restricted evaluation scope: SWE-bench-live filtered to ≤5 files to modify (130 examples, 62 repos), reducing representativeness; single LLM model (GPT-4o) tested; single agentic framework evaluated

Insufficient characterization of when memory helps: High variance in per-instance efficiency (Figure 4) acknowledged but not analyzed; promised agent learning for memory use deferred to future work; error analysis described as small-scale
Incomplete cost-benefit analysis: 4.9% improvement comes with measurable cost increases ($0.54→$0.89 on hard cases); no clear guidance on practical adoption tradeoffs

Underexplored technical results: Dramatic superiority of BM25 over dense retrieval (79.7% vs 73.6% Acc@5) explained speculatively without deep investigation; behavioral shift (Figure 3) analyzed surface-level

Limited experimental breadth: No cross-repository memory transfer exploration; no comparison with simpler memory baselines; generalization beyond code localization unstudied; hyperparameter K sensitivity only on django
